candidates.exact_span: The following Minimum Quantification Levels (MQL's) are to be used for reporting pollutant data for NPDES permit applications and/or compliance reporting.
candidates.computation_change_reason: Whether MQLs govern only permit-application reporting or also compliance reporting affects whether these values set quantification floors for limit-exceedance comparisons (A), whether compliance-reporting obligations incorporate MQL-based reporting rules (B), and how sub-MQL or non-quantified results are classified versus true missing data (C).

Two distinct numeric MQL values are listed for Mercury with a footnote marker but no footnote text in this segment; different readings of which value applies (or what *1 denotes) would change the quantification threshold used for mercury limit comparisons (A) and the missing-evidence classification for mercury results reported near or below those levels (C).

The table's unit designation governs how reported measurements and any permit limits expressed in other units must be converted before numeric compliance comparison; a different unit reading would change exceedance determinations (A).

Separate MQL entries for total cyanide versus weak-acid-dissociable cyanide require matching the correct analyte to the permit's cyanide limit and reported results; misidentifying which cyanide form applies would change applicable quantification thresholds for limit comparison (A) and the semantics of non-quantified cyanide data (C).

The qualifier 'Total Residual Chlorine' distinguishes this parameter from other chlorine forms; applying this MQL to a different chlorine-related limit or measurement would change quantification-based compliance evaluation (A) and classification of sub-MQL chlorine results (C).

This entry specifies an MQL for a single dioxin congener rather than a total-dioxin measure; interpreting whether permit limits and reported results refer to 2,3,7,8-TCDD or a broader dioxin metric would change which quantification floor applies for compliance comparison (A) and how near-detection-limit dioxin evidence is treated (C).
